title: Ataxin-2L Promotes Post-Transcriptional Poly(A) Tail Extension and Translational Activation of Target mRNAs.
abstract: Regulation of mRNA 3' poly(A) tail length plays a central role in post-transcriptional gene regulation by controlling mRNA stability and translational efficiency. Although cytoplasmic polyadenylation has been extensively studied in oocytes and neurons, the mechanisms that mediate post-transcriptional poly(A) tail extension in somatic cells remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify Ataxin-2L as a factor that promotes post-transcriptional poly(A) tail extension and translational activation. Using MS2 tethering assays, we found that recruitment of Ataxin-2L to a reporter mRNA increased mRNA abundance, protein output, and translation efficiency. Northern blot analysis showed that Ataxin-2L promoted poly(A) tail extension even when deadenylation was inhibited by catalytically inactive Caf1 and Pan2 mutants. A transcriptional turn-on assay further demonstrated an increase in poly(A) tail length after transcriptional induction, supporting a role for Ataxin-2L in post-transcriptional polyadenylation. Efficient poly(A) tail extension required the PAM2-mediated interaction with PABPC1 and was reduced by deletion of amino acids 671-842. Ataxin-2L also associated with the cytoplasmic poly(A) polymerase PAPD4/TENT2, and this association remained detectable after deletion of amino acids 671-842. In addition, depletion of Ataxin-2L shortened the poly(A) tail of endogenous NUFIP2 and CUX1 mRNAs. Together, these findings establish Ataxin-2L as a mediator of cytoplasmic poly(A) tail extension and support a broader role for RNA-binding proteins in post-transcriptional polyadenylation in somatic cells.

title: Persistent bilateral STAU1 elevation accompanies increases in p62, GFAP, and phosphorylated tau after traumatic brain injury.
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of long-term neurological disability and increases the risk of neurodegeneration and post-traumatic epileptogenesis. However, the molecular mechanisms responsible for sustained secondary injury and network dysfunction beyond the initial impact remain poorly understood. Staufen-1 (STAU1), an RNA-binding protein that controls mRNA decay, trafficking, and localization to subcellular compartments, is pathologically overabundant in multiple neurodegenerative disease models, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, dementia, and ataxias. Whether STAU1 abundance is altered following moderate controlled cortical impact (CCI), and whether these changes occur alongside increases in p62/SQSTM1, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and phosphorylated tau, remains unknown. Here, using Western blot analyses, we found that STAU1 is persistently elevated in both the ipsilateral hemisphere, including the injury and perilesional regions, and the contralateral cerebrum at 48-h, 1-week, and 1-month post-injury. These increases are accompanied by accumulation of the autophagy adaptor protein p62/SQSTM1, which may suggest changes in p62 synthesis, degradation, or autophagic cargo burden. In parallel, glial fibrillary acidic protein levels as well as phosphorylated tau levels are elevated bilaterally and remain increased 1-month after injury. Together, these findings show a persistent overaccumulation of STAU1 protein levels at several acute time points from 48-h through 1-month after TBI, the first evidence of a previously overlooked factor in the evolving molecular architecture after brain injury. The combination of elevated STAU1, p62, gliosis, and phosphorylated tau in our TBI model provides a basis for future studies on whether STAU1 contributes to injury-associated changes in protein homeostasis and neurological dysfunction, including post-traumatic epilepsy.

title: Argonaute 2 in the Nervous System: Where Causality Is Established in Neurodevelopment and Only Inferred in Neurodegeneration.
abstract: The RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC), built around the Argonaute proteins, executes microRNA-mediated gene silencing. AGO2, the only catalytically active human paralogue, stabilises mature microRNAs in neurons and controls local translation in dendrites and axons. AGO2 is now invoked across the whole span of neurological disease, from monogenic neurodevelopmental syndromes to Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, on evidence of very unequal strength. We therefore ask of each body of work two questions: what was experimentally manipulated, and what was then measured. De novo variants in AGO1 and AGO2 cause the Argonaute syndromes, where the mechanism has been traced from the kinetics of the mutant protein to knock-in mouse phenotypes and indicates delayed strand release rather than loss of function; conditional Ago2 deletion in mice is comparably direct for neurovascular development and adult neurogenesis. In neurodegenerative disease, the position differs. The DISE mechanism shows that AGO2 activity sets the threshold for amyloid-beta toxicity in cultured neurons, and one study identifies AGO2 as an endogenous brake on alpha-synuclein synthesis, but no experiment has yet tested whether altering AGO2 in vivo changes neurodegeneration, even though deleting the upstream enzyme Dicer kills dopaminergic neurons. Benchmarked against TDP-43-dependent mis-splicing, where causality in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is established, AGO2 remains a convergence point for several pathological processes rather than a demonstrated driver of any of them. The available evidence neither establishes nor excludes a causal role, and we set out the experiments that would decide.

title: Fluorescent probes for RNA imaging: illuminating native spatiotemporal dynamics.
abstract: Though recognized as genetic intermediaries, RNA molecules are now established as central regulators of cellular functions. Traditional lysis-based assays provide extensive transcriptomic profiles but fail to preserve the spatiotemporal context of RNA dynamics. To capture these native physiological processes, real-time live-cell fluorescent probes for RNA imaging have emerged as an essential approach. Early imaging strategies relied on cell fixation and bulky tags, introducing methodological artifacts that could mislead biological interpretations. To address these challenges, this review adopts a demand-driven framework by evaluating how specific probe properties are engineered and matched to the biological requirements of a given RNA target and the technical demands of specific imaging goals. Guided by this framework, we outline the evolution and biophysical design principles of fluorescent probes for diverse RNA species and advanced imaging capabilities, including single-molecule imaging, multiplexing, and super-resolution microscopy. In addition, we introduce how probes characterize the binding affinities of RNA-protein interactions (RPIs). These platforms are evaluated against specific biophysical criteria to demonstrate how optimized probe engineering strategies enable researchers to achieve their imaging objectives. By aligning probe design with specific biological questions, we discuss how these platforms uncover novel RNA functions, revolutionize our understanding of RNA dynamics, and advance biomedical research. Finally, we address current bottlenecks in probe performance and envision how interdisciplinary integration will propel RNA imaging beyond observation, establishing a comprehensive and robust toolkit for modeling and translational medicine.

title: Neural stem cell-derived extracellular vesicle non-coding RNAs in cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury: recipient-cell mechanisms, evidence strength, and translational challenges.
abstract: Neural stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles (NSC-EVs) are being studied as cell-free interventions after cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI), but the evidence that a specific non-coding RNA (ncRNA) is the active therapeutic component is uneven. This critical narrative review separates vesicle-associated RNA detection, experimental RNA delivery, target engagement, and cargo-specific causal necessity. An explicitly context-sensitive three-tier framework is applied alongside a domain-by-domain evidence matrix that distinguishes direct ischemia evidence from lineage-adjacent, hypoxia-only, transplantation-associated, and cross-disease observations. Among the studies reviewed, engineered human NSC-EVs enriched with miR-125a-5p provide comparatively direct evidence for IKBKG/NF-κB pathway modulation in a rat transient middle cerebral artery occlusion model; however, effectiveness of engineered loading does not establish that endogenous EV miR-125a-5p is required for unmodified-product activity. The miR-150-3p/CASP2 study supports a neuronal survival mechanism in oxygen-glucose deprivation and an MCAO-associated brain-injury model, without establishing direct microglial reprogramming. miR-362-3p/MCAM/Wnt-β-catenin, miR-9/Hes1, and hNPC-EV miR-100-5p/NOX4 extend the experimental picture toward endogenous repair and vascular responses but retain important limitations in cargo necessity, model match, or cell lineage. hNSC transplantation-associated miR-204-5p/EFNB3 cannot be assumed to represent purified NSC-EV action. Spinal cord injury, miR-124, lncRNA, and circRNA observations are explicitly considered indirect for a CIRI-specific NSC-EV claim. This review identifies experimental design and reporting gaps, distinguishes observed dosing from proposed intervention windows, and outlines falsifiable, rather than clinically established, translational priorities. The updated PubMed and Web of Science export audit identified 150 distinct title/abstract records from 224 primary-database records and additionally highlighted an NSC-EV miR-128-3p/oligodendrocyte progenitor cell repair axis, while preserving a clear distinction between title/abstract screening and definitive full-text causal appraisal.

title: Integrated Bioinformatic Analysis and Preliminary Clinical Validation Reveal a Candidate Diagnostic Immune-Related Gene Signature for Chronic Endometritis.
abstract: Chronic endometritis (CE) is an underdiagnosed condition linked to female infertility. Its immune-related gene (IRG) signature and the mechanisms underlying its immune microenvironment remain unclear. We analyzed mRNA sequencing data from 24 CE and 33 non-CE control endometrial samples, performed differential expression, functional enrichment, and protein-protein interaction analyses, and identified IRGs by intersecting DEGs with the ImmPort database. LASSO, Random Forest, and SVM-RFE were applied to screen for candidate diagnostic IRGs, and diagnostic performance was evaluated via ROC curves, a nomogram, and decision curve analysis in the discovery cohort. Immune cell infiltration was inferred using ssGSEA. Potential drugs and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) were predicted using DSigDB and ENCORI. The expression of the identified IRGs was preliminarily validated by RT-qPCR in an independent clinical cohort. CE tissues exhibited an activated immune profile, notably upregulation of immunoglobulin genes. Four candidate diagnostic IRGs were identified: upregulated IGHV4-34 and RETN, and downregulated F2RL1 and IL6ST. RT-qPCR confirmed the direction of differential expression of these four genes; this preliminary validation supports their potential as candidate biomarkers but does not establish independent diagnostic accuracy. A combined model showed high diagnostic accuracy in the discovery cohort (AUC = 0.907), which may be optimistic and requires independent validation. CE was associated with alterations in inferred immune-cell signatures, including reduced inferred infiltration of plasmacytoid dendritic cells, neutrophils, monocytes, and γδ T cells. F2RL1 and IL6ST expression positively correlated with activated CD8+ T cells and dendritic cells. Drug repositioning suggested indomethacin as a potential therapeutic candidate, and 31 RBPs were predicted to interact with F2RL1 and IL6ST. This exploratory study identifies a candidate 4-IRG signature for CE and provides preliminary RT-qPCR expression validation. The findings suggest an altered endometrial immune landscape and raise the hypothesis that the F2RL1/IL6ST axis may be involved in CE immunopathology, providing new insights for diagnosis and therapy.

title: ADAR2 suppresses bladder cancer metastasis by binding and destabilizing FASN mRNA in an RNA editing-independent manner.
abstract: Bladder cancer (BCa) metastasis remains a major challenge to patient survival, and the underlying mechanisms have not been fully elucidated. Although the ADAR family has been implicated in tumor biology, the role of ADAR2 in BCa metastasis remains unclear. ADAR2 expression in BCa was analyzed using TCGA datasets and validated by quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR) in 40 pairs of BCa and adjacent normal tissues. Functional effects were investigated using in vitro migration and invasion assays and in vivo mouse models of popliteal lymph node and lung metastasis. Mechanistic studies included mRNA sequencing, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS), Nile Red staining, free fatty acid (FFA) quantification, RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP), rescue assays using editing-domain mutants, and actinomycin D chase assays to investigate the regulation of fatty acid synthase (FASN) and fatty acid synthesis. ADAR2 was downregulated in BCa tissues, and its expression was positively associated with an improved patient prognosis. Functionally, ADAR2 inhibited BCa cell migration and invasion in vitro, as demonstrated by Transwell migration, Matrigel invasion, and wound-healing assays, and in vivo, as demonstrated using popliteal lymph node and lung metastasis models. Integrated analysis of mRNA-sequencing data, together with Nile Red staining, Oil Red O staining, and FFA quantification, revealed that ADAR2 reduced cytoplasmic FFA accumulation by downregulating FASN. Mechanistically, the absence of detectable A-to-I editing in FASN exons and the inability of the catalytically inactive ADAR2E396A mutant to rescue FASN expression indicated an editing-independent mechanism. Actinomycin D chase, dual-luciferase reporter, and RIP assays demonstrated that ADAR2 acted as an RNA-binding protein (RBP) that bound to the FASN mRNA 3' UTR, destabilized the transcript, and thereby downregulated FASN expression. ADAR2 inhibited BCa cell migration and invasion by downregulating FASN-mediated fatty acid synthesis through an RNA editing-independent pathway.

title: Biophysical Characterization of ParBS Condensates suggests a physical mechanism for segregation
abstract: The ParABS system orchestrates chromosome segregation in many bacterial species. The centromere-like parS sites serve as nucleation points for the binding of the ParB protein. Subsequent diffusion on adjacent, non-specific DNA regions (spreading) in the presence of CTP and binding of more ParB molecules along with DNA looping via ParB-ParB interactions bring distal parts of the chromosome into proximity. ParB interaction with the ParA-ATPase motor protein, then, drives genomic segregation. It has been shown that in some bacterial species, the ParB-parS complex undergoes phase separation into a condensate. However, the physico-chemical properties of such condensates and their response to forces, such as those they may face in the cell, have not yet been characterized. Performing turbidity measurements in the presence of CTP, various concentrations of DNA and physiological mono and divalent salt, it was shown that Mg2+ facilitates, while K+ concentrations higher than ~20 mM disfavor, condensate formation. Micro rheology measurements showed that condensates of ParB and DNA including parS sites (ParB-parS DNA) in the presence of CTP, are viscoelastic with a viscosity at Troom of ~5 Pa s and able to respond to deformations with a network relaxation time of 0.1 s. Additionally, fluorescence combined with force spectroscopy showed that mechanical disruption of ParB-DNA condensates in the presence of CTP requires 5-7.5 pN of tension in the DNA, which is lower than the force required to stall a molecular motor such as RNA polymerase, but higher than the force required for the relocation of chromosomes and plasmids during segregation. These results support the idea that ParB-parS condensates dynamically rearrange at the molecular level while maintaining the cohesion necessary to sustain the drag force of segregation without interfering with genomic transactions. This physical mechanism could be the basis for the critical role of ParB-parS condensates in organizing and partitioning bacterial chromosomes.

title: The Sec61-EMC complex promotes biosynthesis of the SARS-CoV-2 non-structural proteins.
abstract: The genomic RNA of SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for the global COVID-19 pandemic, encodes polyproteins pp1a and pp1ab which contain 16 non-structural proteins (NSPs) that support critical steps in infection. Despite this, how the polyproteins are synthesized and membrane-inserted in the host cell is unclear. Here we demonstrate that SARS-CoV-2 exploits the Sec61-endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane complex (EMC) translation machinery to promote biosynthesis of the virus polyproteins, leading to successful replication and infection. The Sec61-EMC complex engages NSP3-the first transmembrane (TM) protein in pp1a/pp1ab-during active translation. Strikingly, of the four TM segments in NSP3, a marginally hydrophobic domain between TM3 and TM4 is required for EMC-binding and confers EMC-dependent expression. Our results reveal an ER-dependent mechanism for translation of the SARS-CoV-2 NSPs during virus infection, providing insights that should lead to new anti-SARS-CoV-2 therapeutic approaches.

title: Unloaded Nanoarchaeosomes Increase the Expression of COMMD5 and SLC25A10 Genes in Caco-2 Cells.
abstract: Targeted delivery of therapeutic agents using lipid vesicles is an important area of modern biomedicine. However, the intrinsic biological effects of such carriers on cells require further investigation. Nanoarchaeosomes represent one promising class of delivery vehicles. In the present study, we investigated the response of Caco-2 intestinal epithelial cells to unloaded nanoarchaeosomes. Their exposure was accompanied by pronounced remodeling of several transcriptional programs. Enrichment of genes associated with the lysosomal pathway was observed. Carbohydrate and lipid metabolism were activated, including glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway, triacylglycerol synthesis, and glycosphingolipid metabolism. In contrast, nanoarchaeosome treatment suppressed transcriptional programs related to the cell cycle, including the G2/M transition and E2F- and MYC-dependent programs, as well as RNA splicing and protein secretion. At the individual gene level, increased expression of COMMD5, which is associated with endosomal trafficking, and SLC25A10, which transports malate and succinate across the inner mitochondrial membrane, was observed. Thus, unloaded nanoarchaeosomes are not biologically inert toward Caco-2 cells and induce a complex adaptive transcriptional response, which should be taken into account when interpreting the effects of encapsulated small molecules and nucleic acids.

title: Heat-Inactivated Akkermansia muciniphila Reduces Viability Under Non-Adherent Conditions and Alters MUC13 and Survival-Related Gene Expression in Colorectal Cancer Cells.
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) progression and metastasis are driven by molecular mechanisms that promote cell survival, migration, and resistance to anoikis. Current evidence indicates that the gut microbiota can actively influence these processes. Therefore, the main goal of this study was to investigate the impact of Akkermansia muciniphila on CRC aggressiveness by assessing gene expression, migration, and anoikis. Based on our previously reported cytotoxicity findings, human CRC cell lines derived from primary and metastatic tumors were treated with a heat-inactivated A. muciniphila preparation alone or in combination with 5-fluorouracil. Following treatment, RNA and protein were extracted for molecular analyses. Migration and sensitivity to anoikis were analyzed using wound-healing and anoikis assays, respectively. Gene expression analysis was performed to assess key survival and metastatic regulators. Our results showed that at the molecular level, heat-inactivated A. muciniphila preparation reduced the aberrant expression of MUC13, a protein associated with anoikis resistance, and suppressed several critical genes involved in the MAPK and PI3K/AKT signaling pathways, including KRAS, MEK1, and PIK3CA, while restoring the expression of the tumor suppressor gene PTEN. At the functional level, heat-inactivated A. muciniphila preparation significantly reduced cell migration and enhanced sensitivity to anoikis. Overall, this study demonstrates that heat-inactivated A. muciniphila preparation may limit colorectal cancer progression through the inhibition of migration, restoration of anoikis sensitivity, and modulation of oncogenic signaling pathways at multiple levels. In conclusion, our findings highlight the potential of A. muciniphila as a complementary therapeutic approach that may enhance the effectiveness of colorectal cancer treatment and help limit metastatic progression. However, further in vivo studies are needed to validate these results and guide future research.

title: Lipid Nanoparticle-mRNA Vaccines for Infectious Diseases: Making a Potent Platform Predictable.
abstract: Lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-mRNA vaccines compressed the path from pathogen sequence to licensed product into less than a year and are now approved for three viral diseases (COVID-19, respiratory syncytial virus and seasonal influenza), with more than twenty indications in clinical development. The platform's potency is no longer in doubt; its predictability is. We argue that progress is now limited by three interfaces that are engineered largely independently: the lipid-RNA interface, which sets encapsulation, internal structure and storage stability; the particle-cell interface, which sets tropism and the efficiency of endosomal escape; and the particle-immune interface, which sets the balance between adjuvanticity and reactogenicity. Quantitative design rules exist for the first interface, remain empirical for the second, and are almost absent for the third, which is why formulation development still proceeds by screening rather than by calculation. We review the molecular design of the mRNA payload and structural antigen selection; the chemistry, manufacture and intracellular trafficking of LNPs; the immunological chain that links innate activation and dendritic-cell cross-presentation to germinal-centre output; and the clinical evidence across COVID-19, respiratory syncytial virus, influenza, cytomegalovirus, HIV, personalised cancer vaccines and other targets. We conclude by identifying the measurements, pharmacopoeial quality attributes and design rules that would make the next generation of LNP-mRNA vaccines predictable rather than empirical.

title: Evaluating a Potential Dose-Sparing Self-Amplifying RNA Vaccine for Induction of Functional Antibodies to Blood-Stage Plasmodium falciparum Malaria.
abstract: Introduction: Next-generation malaria vaccines are urgently needed to provide greater efficacy and longevity. Antibodies targeting blood-stage merozoites can confer protection against clinical malaria through multiple Fc-mediated functions. In particular, merozoite surface protein 2 (PfMSP2) is a known target of protective antibodies that can clear merozoites via multiple antibody Fc-mediated functions, making it a highly promising vaccine candidate. Methods: We developed PfMSP2 as a self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) vaccine, which was successfully validated for in vitro expression in mammalian cells. Subsequently, the PfMSP2-saRNA was formulated as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and evaluated for immunogenicity in mice following a three-dose regimen comparing 1 μg and 10 μg doses. We evaluated the induction of antibodies with functional activities relevant to protective immunity. Results: Our PfMSP2-saRNA vaccine induced antigen-specific IgG responses that recognised the surface of whole merozoites. Both 1 μg and 10 μg dosing regimens induced comparable antibodies to PfMSP2, and responses were predominantly murine cytophilic IgG subclasses. These vaccine-induced antibodies demonstrated potent Fc-mediated functions, including complement fixation and binding of human Fcγ-receptor I (FcγRI), after only two doses, which remained consistent after the third dose. Conclusions: PfMSP2 is highly immunogenic using the saRNA vaccine platform in a potential dose-sparing regimen, and induces antibodies with multiple Fc-mediated functions associated with protective immunity in humans. This saRNA platform is a promising strategy to develop highly efficacious vaccines requiring lower and fewer doses.

title: Functional Analysis of Schistosoma japonicum Aminopeptidase N.
abstract: Schistosoma japonicum aminopeptidase N (SjAPN) is a conserved M1 family metalloprotease, but its role in schistosome biology remains unclear. Bioinformatics analysis, quantitative PCR, RNA interference, confocal microscopy, and scanning electron microscopy were used to characterize SjAPN expression and function. SjAPN contained typical metalloprotease domains and showed high sequence similarity to homologs from other trematodes. Its transcription increased during schistosome development, was higher in female worms than in males, and was mainly detected in the anterior region of both sexes. RNA interference effectively reduced SjAPN transcript levels in adult worms. Functional analysis showed that SjAPN silencing was associated with reduced egg output during in vitro culture, altered vitellocyte staining, and tegumental surface changes in female worms. In the in vivo experiment, worm burden was significantly lower in the SjAPN RNAi group than in the NC group, but not in the PBS group. These findings indicate that SjAPN transcript levels are associated with changes in the development and reproductive biology of S. japonicum, particularly in female worms, and may be a potential target for further studies on schistosome control. Further studies are required to determine whether these phenotypes are mediated by reduced SjAPN protein abundance or enzymatic activity.

title: Characterization and Evaluation of the Neuroprotective Potential of Peptides Derived from Holothuria scabra Inner Wall Proteins: An In Vitro Study.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are characterized by progressive neuronal dysfunction driven by interconnected mechanisms, including oxidative stress, apoptosis, and impaired protein homeostasis. Marine-derived proteins and peptides represent promising sources of multifunctional neuroprotective agents; however, the neuroprotective potential of gastrointestinal digestion-derived peptides from Holothuria scabra remains poorly characterized. This study investigated the neuroprotective effects of a gastrointestinal digest of H. scabra inner-wall proteins (IWD), a mixture of digestion-derived peptides, in an OA-induced SH-SY5Y cell model. The original protein extract (IW) was characterized by LC-MS/MS and PANTHER, while IWD-derived peptides were profiled by LC-MS/MS and evaluated using in silico bioactivity and ADMET prediction. In vitro, IWD pretreatment significantly attenuated OA-induced neuronal injury by reducing intracellular ROS accumulation while preserving cell viability and neuronal morphology; 5 μg/mL showed the strongest protective effect. Proteomic analysis identified STMN1 as a major discriminator associated with neuronal structural adaptation, while RPS27A and RPLP2 were associated with translational regulation. HSPB1, HSP90AB1, and PARK7 emerged as additional candidate proteins related to cellular stress responses and homeostasis. Integrated proteomic and network analyses further highlighted proteins associated with ribosomal function, RNA processing, and proteostasis. These findings suggest that IWD-associated neuroprotection involves coordinated changes in neuronal structure and cellular maintenance pathways, supporting further validation of H. scabra-derived peptides as potential neuroprotective candidates.

title: Transient RNA-Based AID-Cas9 Editing Enables Efficient Gene and Splice-Site Modification.
abstract: Transient RNA delivery offers a practical approach to programmable genome editing without introducing editor-encoding DNA, but editing performance depends on reagent design, delivery conditions, and target accessibility. Here, we evaluated an RNA-based editing workflow built around a cytosine base editor derived from targeted activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID)-mediated mutagenesis (TAM). Systematic adjustment of editor mRNA and guide RNA dosage, poly(A) tail configuration, and untranslated regions identified parameters influencing cytosine-to-thymine conversion; viability remained high at 24 h under the tested RNA-dose conditions. Further optimized electroporation enabled efficient reporter mRNA delivery into primary human CD8+ T cells. In two independent donor experiments, targeted nucleotide conversion at the endogenous CD3E locus and the CD3-negative fraction were higher after sequential than after single electroporation. To investigate splice-site editing, we screened AID-Cas9 combinations targeting the mouse Nr4a2 exon 3 splice acceptor and generated mutant mice through embryo editing and subsequent breeding. Sanger sequencing of genomic DNA from primary CD8+ T cells confirmed the intended Nr4a2 splice-site mutation, while Hi-TOM-based targeted cDNA amplicon sequencing revealed altered splice-junction patterns, including the emergence of an unexpected splice junction in mutant cells. However, no statistically significant differences in tumor progression were detected in the B16-OVA adoptive transfer or B16F10 tumor models. Together, these findings provide a practical framework for transient RNA-based base editing in primary T cells and targeted modification of splice-regulatory sequences, while highlighting the complexity of splice-site editing outcomes.

title: Virus-Induced Plant Genome Editing: Four Delivery Architectures and Their Trade-Offs.
abstract: Plant genome editing has been limited by the difficulty of delivering CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats) reagents to germline-competent cells without stable transgene integration. Viral vectors address this by exploiting endogenous replication, cell-to-cell movement and phloem transport, but cargo capacity and germline access have so far traded against each other. We classify virus-induced genome editing (VIGE) systems along two binary design choices: whether the vector itself encodes the nuclease and whether an engineered mobility mechanism carries the editing reagents to the germline. These two axes define four delivery architectures: (a) guide-only without a mobility element, in which guides are delivered into a nuclease-expressing host; (b) guide-only with a mobile RNA element that carries the guide into meristematic cells, yielding heritable edits without tissue culture; (c) nuclease-encoding without a route to the germline, achieved by shrinking the nuclease or enlarging the vector; and (d) nuclease-encoding with a mobility element, reaching the germline directly. We evaluate all four architectures against three persistent constraints. These are off-target risks from viral amplification of the editing reagents, the host range of the available vectors, and the gap between model-system demonstrations and breeding pipelines. Finally, we propose that combining engineered compact nucleases, mobile RNA signals, and morphogenic regulators could enable a single-vector pipeline for producing edited seeds. This would extend genome editing to refractory crop species and reduce reliance on tissue-culture-based transformation.

title: Effects of the Antivitamin Roseoflavin on the Structure of the RNA-Derived Bacterial Community in Pooled Human Saliva: An Exploratory In Vitro Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives: The antivitamin roseoflavin is a structural analogue of riboflavin and may affect oral bacterial communities through competitive antagonism. Methods: In this exploratory in vitro study, saliva from 14 volunteers was pooled before allocation to the experimental conditions and incubated for 24 h with roseoflavin or ampicillin. RNA was isolated and RNA-derived bacterial community profiles were analyzed by 16S rRNA sequencing using QIIME 2 and ANCOM-BC2. Because all experimental replicates originated from a single pooled biological source, the findings do not support donor-level or population-level inference. Results: Total RNA levels and alpha diversity showed treatment-associated tendencies, with the strongest reduction after ampicillin treatment; however, these differences were not statistically significant. Beta diversity indicated modest treatment-associated variation within the pooled experimental system. Differential abundance analysis indicated moderate shifts in the relative representation of taxa within the RNA-derived oral bacterial community. Valid ANCOM-BC2-derived log2 fold change estimates for both vehicle-matched treatment comparisons were obtained for 45 taxonomic units. Most taxa showed concordant directional responses to roseoflavin and ampicillin, whereas only a small subset showed treatment-specific descriptive patterns. Ampicillin tended to induce larger absolute log2 fold changes than roseoflavin. Conclusions: Within this pooled exploratory model, roseoflavin treatment was associated with moderate shifts in the RNA-derived oral bacterial community rather than broad community-wide changes. Whether the comparatively limited response reflects selective activity, insufficient antimicrobial potency, community-level buffering, or a combination of these mechanisms remains unresolved. The findings require validation using independent donors, controlled dose-response experiments, and more physiologically relevant oral models.

title: Comparative pan-genomics reveals extensive variation in secondary metabolism and the non-coding repertoire of clinically relevant Fusarium solani species complex members.
abstract: The Fusarium solani species complex (FSSC) is a group of dual-kingdom fungal pathogens capable of causing devastating disease on a wide range of host plants and life-threatening infections in humans that are difficult to treat. In this study, we generate highly contiguous genomes for three clinical isolates each of Fusarium keratoplasticum and Fusarium petroliphilum and compare them with others of the FSSC from plant and animal sources. We find no clear host specialization within the complex, with isolates from plant and animal sources being intermixed on the phylogeny. Pangenome analysis revealed extensive gene presence-absence, with only 41% of genes found in all samples and accessory chromosomes encoding isolate- and species-specific genes. Definition of long non-coding RNAs in F. keratoplasticum and F. petroliphilum demonstrated that they show a similarly high degree of presence-absence variation but are integrated into the transcriptional network to a similar degree as protein-coding genes, suggesting broad and extensive cellular roles, including secondary metabolism. Finally, examination of the FSSC for gigantic Starship mobile genetic elements revealed that two-thirds of the samples analyzed harbored at least one element. However, the cargo contained within these elements was largely isolate-specific, highlighting their role in contributing to the high degree of gene content variation observed. This study provides valuable insights into the evolutionary dynamics and genomic architecture of the FSSC, with implications for understanding its generalist nature and multi-kingdom virulence, something of increasing relevance as climate change potentially increases the number of fungal species that can grow at human temperatures.IMPORTANCEThe Fusarium solani species complex is a group of fungi capable of destroying important crops and causing human infections that are often antifungal resistant. While the magnitude of disease in both the plant and animal kingdom is apparent, we are currently lacking a data set to characterize the genomic diversity that likely underpins its fitness in such different hosts. This study generates six highly contiguous clinical genomes of F. keratoplasticum and F. petroliphilum and compares them against other Fusarium solani species complex members, finding tremendous differences in gene content between isolates and species. Through definition of the secondary metabolic potential, long non-coding RNAs, and Starship mobile genetic elements, we begin to unravel the forces that cause such tremendous genetic diversity, and their potential consequences for both human and plant infection.

title: First metagenomic detection and partial genomic characterization of Bossavirus delphinidgamma1 in captive common bottlenose dolphins in Southeast Asia.
abstract: Bossavirus delphinidgamma1 is a dolphin-associated gammaherpesvirus for which genomic information from tropical Asian marine mammal populations remains scarce. This study aimed to detect and partially characterize Bossavirus delphinidgamma1 in captive common bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus) in Indonesia and evaluate an integrated Oxford Nanopore Flongle-Illumina sequencing workflow for viral surveillance using non-invasive, low-biomass samples. Fifteen blowhole, anal, and reproductive tract swabs were collected from five clinically healthy captive dolphins between January 2023 and January 2025. RNA and DNA were extracted from individual or pooled samples. RNA underwent sequence-independent single-primer amplification followed by Oxford Nanopore Flongle sequencing, whereas DNA from Dolphin 4 was sequenced using Illumina NovaSeq X. Metagenomic reads were subjected to taxonomic identification, reference mapping, consensus generation, coding sequence annotation, protein similarity analysis, multiple-sequence alignment, and maximum-likelihood phylogenetic analysis. Oxford Nanopore sequencing detected Bossavirus delphinidgamma1 sequences exclusively in the anal swab from Dolphin 4. The run generated 87,070 reads, of which 109 (0.12%) mapped to the viral reference genome, with a mean coverage depth of 0.28×. Subsequent DNA metagenomic sequencing of pooled Dolphin 4 swab extracts confirmed viral genetic material. Combined Oxford Nanopore and Illumina mapping covered 63.7% of the reference genome, with a median depth of 1×; 0.71% of the genome achieved ≥10× coverage. The recovered sequence contained a nearly complete DE1 gene and >50% coverage of several additional coding regions. Twelve predicted coding regions showed 68.9%-97.1% amino acid identity to Bossavirus delphinidgamma1 or a closely related dolphin gammaherpesvirus. Phylogenetic analysis placed the Indonesian sequence with the Sarasota reference strain, with 100% bootstrap support. This study provides the first metagenomic evidence and partial genomic characterization of Bossavirus delphinidgamma1 in captive common bottlenose dolphins in Indonesia and Southeast Asia. The integrated sequencing approach enabled substantial partial-genome recovery from non-invasive samples and supports its application for exploratory marine mammal viral surveillance. Larger longitudinal studies incorporating targeted molecular confirmation, serology, and environmental sampling are warranted.

title: Discovery of SARS-CoV-2 Nsp14 Methyltransferase Inhibitors with Potent Antiviral Activity.
abstract: To pursue SARS-CoV-2 nsp14 methyltransferase (MTase) inhibitors as COVID-19 therapeutics, we have performed structure-activity relationship studies on prototypic bisubstrate inhibitor 5, exploring the sulfonamide linker, nucleobase and ribose ring. Our work has led to multiple potent inhibitors including 28, which has an antiviral EC50 value of 90 nM (in A549 ACE2/TMPRSS2 cells) and a high selectivity index (CC50/EC50). Furthermore, we have established that selected compounds are highly selective over human RNA MTase hRNMT. Also importantly, we have shown that compound 28 inhibits nsp14 MTases from MERS-CoV and bat SARS-like coronavirus SHC014-CoV. However, we have also witnessed the complexity of simultaneous optimization of antiviral potency and drug-like properties. Overall, our work strongly supports nsp14 MTase inhibitor discovery as a promising strategy to combat SARS-CoV-2 and other coronaviruses of pandemic potential.

title: Dendritic cell-targeting virus-like particles as mRNA carriers induce Th1-skewed humoral and cellular immunity.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines have emerged as a powerful vaccination platform, yet efficient and targeted delivery of mRNA to professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs) remains a major challenge. Here, we developed a dendritic cell (DC)-targeting virus-like particle (DVLP) platform for mRNA delivery by combining human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) Gag fused with the bacteriophage MS2 coat protein, which recognizes mRNA bearing MS2 stem-loop sequences and an engineered Sindbis virus glycoprotein mutant (SV-Gmt) that preferentially targets dendritic cells. African swine fever virus (ASFV) P30 was employed as a model antigen to evaluate platform performance. In vitro, SV-Gmt-pseudotyped VLPs encapsulating P30 mRNA (DVLP-P30) preferentially delivered antigen mRNA to dendritic cells compared with broad-tropic vesicular stomatitis virus G protein (VSV-G)-pseudotyped VLPs encapsulating P30 mRNA (VSV-G VLP-P30). In mice, vaccination with DVLP-P30 induced significantly higher P30-specific antibody responses than VSV-G VLP-P30. Enhanced humoral immunity was accompanied by increased frequencies of CD4+ and CD8+ effector memory T cells, indicating improved generation of antigen-specific immune memory. Notably, DC-targeted mRNA delivery promoted stronger interferon-γ responses and increased IgG2a production, consistent with a Type 1 helper T cell (Th1)-skewed immune profile. Together, these findings demonstrate that DC-targeting VLPs function as effective mRNA carriers and enhance both the magnitude and quality of vaccine-induced immunity. This work establishes a versatile platform for targeted mRNA delivery and supports further development of DVLPs for prophylactic and therapeutic vaccination.

title: Effects of different doses of Poly I:C on immune responses and protective efficacy induced by intranasal immunization with HRSV pre-F protein in mice.
abstract: Human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) primarily infects the respiratory mucosa, making local mucosal immunity an important target for vaccine development. Poly I:C is a promising mucosal adjuvant, but the effects of different doses on immune responses and protection induced by intranasal HRSV prefusion F (Pre-F) protein vaccination remain unclear. Female BALB/c mice were assigned to five groups (n = 6 per group): Pre-F + 10 μg CpG, Pre-F + 10 μg Poly I:C, Pre-F + 25 μg Poly I:C, Pre-F + 50 μg Poly I:C, and PBS. Mice were immunized intranasally on days 0 and 21. Serum Pre-F-specific antibodies and HRSV-neutralizing antibodies were measured after the second immunization. Mice were challenged intranasally with HRSV Long strain 14 days after the second immunization. Body weight, splenic cytokine-secreting lymphocytes, lung Pre-F-specific IgA, HRSV RNA loads, and lung histopathology were evaluated. All immunized groups developed Pre-F-specific antibody responses. Neutralizing antibody titers in the 10, 25, and 50 μg Poly I:C groups were 262, 340, and 1,173, respectively, while lung Pre-F-specific IgA titers were 1,185, 1,405, and 1,838. All Poly I:C groups induced IFN-γ-secreting lymphocyte responses, with the strongest response observed in the 50 μg group. Following HRSV challenge, immunized mice showed less body weight loss, lower lung HRSV RNA loads, and reduced histopathological injury than PBS controls. Among the Poly I:C groups, the 50 μg group had the lowest lung HRSV RNA load (30.6 copies/mg), approximately 1/25 of that in the PBS group (766.5 copies/mg). Poly I:C enhanced systemic, mucosal, and cellular immune responses induced by intranasal HRSV Pre-F immunization and improved protection against HRSV challenge. Within the tested dose range, 50 μg Poly I:C showed the most favorable overall profile among the Poly I:C groups and warrants further dose-optimization and safety evaluation.

title: A Naturally Occurring Amino Acid Variation in the Cucumber Mosaic Virus 2b Protein Modulates Silencing Suppression, Virulence and Leaf Deformity.
abstract: Virus-induced symptoms that develop on infected plants are often very specific; however, the molecular background of these symptoms usually remains unknown with very few exceptions. Here, we studied the molecular background of severe symptoms induced by the ScL strain of Cucumber mosaic virus (ScL-CMV). Using chimaeras of ScL-CMV and another subgroup II strain, Trk7-CMV, we identified the 2b silencing suppressor gene as the primary determinant of symptom severity. A single amino acid change at position 14 (H14Q) in the 2b protein was sufficient to convert a weak silencing suppressor from Trk7-CMV into a potent one, as observed in ScL-CMV. This variation likely impacts protein stability within the plant, and influences its silencing suppression capacity. Furthermore, we demonstrated that ScL-CMV infection disrupts the biogenesis of tasi-ARF, a small RNA involved in regulating plant development. This disruption is associated with increased expression of the target gene, AUXIN RESPONSE FACTOR 4 (ARF4), a key regulator of leaf polarity. The misregulation of ARF4 may contribute to the severe leaf deformation observed in ScL-CMV-infected plants.

title: Hypothalamic delivery of self-assembled Ampkα1 siRNA via host extracellular vesicles treats obesity.
abstract: Obesity remains a significant global health issue characterized by complex pathophysiology and severe metabolic complications. Genetic suppression of AMP-activated protein kinase alpha 1 (Ampkα1) in steroidogenic factor 1 (SF1) neurons of the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) promote feeding-independent obesity resistance by activating brown adipose tissue (BAT) thermogenesis via uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1). While RNA interference (RNAi) offers precision in modulating such targets, translating oligonucleotide therapies for neurological applications has been impeded by inefficient in vivo delivery, poor blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration and off-target toxicity. Here, we report a non-viral RNA interference strategy combining small interfering RNA (siRNA) targeting hypothalamic Ampkα1 with a tissue-engineered platform that exploits host tissues as in vivo biogenerators. By leveraging small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) derived from host tissue, our approach achieves brain gene silencing while circumventing the limitations of conventional delivery systems. Notably, this strategy predominantly suppressed Ampkα1 in the SF1 neurons of the VMH of C57BL/6J mice, stimulating BAT thermogenesis and metabolic activation with minimal off-target effects and no detectable adverse effects-enabling a potent, feeding-independent anti-obesity intervention. Moreover, in order to avoid multiple administration of regular gene vector, we designed minicircle vectors that achieved sustained siRNA expression, resulting in significant weight loss for over a week from a single dose. Overall, our findings establish a safe, durable and effective siRNA delivery paradigm, positioning it as a next-generation RNAi therapeutic to address obesity and related metabolic disorders.

title: Increased synapse elimination by inflammatory cells contributes to long-lasting post-stroke memory dysfunction in old mice.
abstract: Post-stroke memory dysfunction is common in elderly people. We showed previously that a bone fracture (BF) shortly before ischemic stroke also caused long-lasting memory dysfunction in young mice, and inhibition of inflammation by α7-nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (α7-nAChR) agonist treatment alleviated their cognitive deficit. Excessive synapse removal by glial cells contributes to neuronal network disruption and neurobehavioral deficits during the acute and subacute stages of stroke. However, its role at the chronic stage of stroke remains unclear. In this study, we analyzed the impact of microglia- and astrocyte-mediated synapse removal at the chronic stage of ischemic stroke on memory function and synapse structure in young (2-month-old) and old mice (15-18-month-old). We also tested whether α7-nAChR agonist treatment reduced synapse loss in young mice with BF+stroke. Ischemic stroke was induced by permanent occlusion of the distal middle cerebral artery (dMCAO). The BF model was induced by creating a tibia fracture under aseptic conditions 6 h before dMCAO. An α7-nAChR agonist was administered immediately before BF and 1 day after dMCAO. Memory function was evaluated weekly for 8 weeks using the Y-maze test and the novel object recognition test one week before and 8 weeks after dMCAO. Atrophic volumes, synapse-engulfing astrocytes and microglia/macrophages, RNA expression profiles, neurite length, and dendritic spine density were analyzed in the peri-atrophic regions and hippocampal regions eight weeks after dMCAO. Old mice developed long-lasting memory dysfunction (> eight weeks), had larger atrophic volumes, shorter neurite length, and fewer dendritic spines, accompanied by increased synapse-engulfing astrocytes and microglia/macrophages in the peri-atrophic and hippocampal regions than young stroke-only mice. Old stroke mice showed higher upregulation of inflammatory pathways and more downregulation of neurite growth and synaptic transmission pathways than in young stroke-only mice. Young mice with BF+stroke had more synapse-engulfing astrocytes and microglia/macrophages in the hippocampal regions than in young stroke-only mice. An α7-nAChR agonist treatment reduced synapse-engulfing microglia/macrophages and astrocytes in the hippocampi of BF+stroke mice. Enhanced synapse elimination contributes to the long-lasting post-stroke memory dysfunction. Inhibition of neuroinflammation at the early stage of stroke can reduce synapse loss and improve post-stroke memory function.

title: Post-testicular sperm maturation and psychological stress.
abstract: Stressors encountered in the paternal preconception environment have been linked both to impaired male fertility and to an increased risk of developing disease states among offspring, the latter owing to the transmission of epigenetic information via the exposed male germline. Psychological stress is among the most prevalent of these exposures and is thought to act on the male reproductive tract through glucocorticoid signalling, but mechanistic understanding of how stress-responsive epigenetic signals are transmitted to the spermatozoa and the importance of the timing and extent of the exposure remains limited. Among the developmental windows during which stress signals could be relayed to spermatozoa, increasing evidence has implicated transit through the epididymis. Epididymal spermatozoa are transcriptionally and translationally inert, so any changes must occur independently of de novo RNA and protein synthesis. By contrast, the transfer of small non-coding RNAs provides an opportunity for rapid changes to the sperm epigenetic profile following even relatively short-term exposure to stressors. Thus, altered sperm small non-coding RNA cargo has increasingly been suggested as a mechanism that can propagate increased risk of disease in offspring.

title: ​mRNA-based Medical Countermeasures for CBRN threats: Current Status and Research Priorities.
abstract: Medical countermeasures (MCM) for chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) threats have relied on recombinant protein therapeutics and monoclonal antibodies, which are constrained by slow, costly, and difficult-to-scale manufacturing. mRNA platforms offer a potentially faster and more scalable route to vaccines, therapeutic enzymes, antibodies, and other biologics against CBRN threats, but introduce their own translational barriers, including cold-chain logistics, dose-response uncertainty, and organ-specific delivery. This review evaluates the current status of mRNA-based MCMs organized around the three core CBRN threat pillars, chemical, biological, and radiological/nuclear, using chemical defense bioscavengers, a nerve agent MCM with the most mature mechanistic foundation but the least translation to mRNA-based formats, as an anchor case. Within each pillar we distinguish clinically evaluated approaches from preclinical proof-of-concept studies and from conceptual extensions for which no mRNA-specific data yet exist, and we critically assess translational feasibility and field-deployment barriers rather than only cataloguing potential applications. We close with cross-cutting research gaps in RNA stability, dosing, organ-targeted delivery, and distributed field manufacturing that must be addressed before mRNA MCMs can be fielded.

title: Nascent RNA-mediated recruitment and R-loop suppression underlie FUS-driven enhancement of transcription.
abstract: Biomolecular condensates have been proposed to enhance transcription by locally concentrating polymerases and cofactors, often through intrinsically disordered proteins. However, the functional role of phase separation and the molecular connections between RNA and the transcription machinery remain poorly defined. Using T7 RNA polymerase (T7 RNAP), which lacks intrinsic disorder, together with FUS, which does not directly interact with T7 RNAP, we dissect the mechanisms by which FUS enhances transcription. We find that monomeric FUS is sufficient to stimulate transcription, whereas condensate formation contributes only a modest additional effect. FUS is recruited selectively to active transcription complexes through binding to nascent RNA, assembling into a dynamic nanoscale structure that enhances RNAP loading and stabilizes the transcription initiation bubble. Furthermore, FUS suppresses inhibitory R-loop formation, thereby accelerating elongation. Together, these findings identify nascent RNA as the central organizing element through which FUS modulates transcription via specific molecular interactions, largely independent of phase separation.

title: A tri-modular feline infectious peritonitis virus nanoparticle vaccine confers complete protection in female cats without detectable antibody-dependent enhancement.
abstract: Antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) complicates coronavirus vaccine development. Feline infectious peritonitis virus (FIPV) is a classic model of coronavirus vaccine-mediated ADE. Here, we develop ferritin-based FIPV nanoparticle vaccines displaying nucleocapsid (N) antigen, antigen-presenting cell (APC)-targeting ligands, and immunostimulatory factors, and evaluate their protective efficacy, serum-mediated ADE risk, and associated immune features. Compared with soluble N protein, the single-module FIPV N nanoparticle vaccine (sfNnps) enhances FIPV N-specific T-cell responses yet confers only 25.0% (2/8) protection. Dual-module vaccines incorporating either the APC-targeting ligand HCV E2 (dfN/Hnps) or the immunostimulatory factor IFNγ (dfN/Inps) further boost N-specific T-cell responses and confer 50.0% (4/8) and 62.5% (5/8) protection, respectively. The tri-modular vaccine co-displaying N, HCV E2, and IFNγ (tfN/HInps) elicits the most robust N-specific T-cell responses and affords 100% (8/8) protection in female cats, while showing no detectable serum-mediated ADE under the tested conditions and reducing peripheral-blood viral RNA levels by 73.0%. Immune profiling associates tfN/HInps with increased cDC1 representation and antigen-presentation gene expression, as well as a shift toward CD8⁺ effector-memory T cells and a FOXO1-centered program linked to transcriptional features of increased proliferation, memory formation, and cytotoxicity. Overall, this engineered FIPV nano‑display vaccine could provide a framework for cellular‑immunity‑oriented vaccine development against ADE‑prone coronaviruses.

title: tsRNA-3012b couples m7G-associated IGF2BP3-BCKDK signaling to NADK-dependent NADP(H) metabolism in cystitis glandularis.
abstract: How post-transcriptional regulation couples NADP(H) metabolism to epithelial proliferation in cystitis glandularis (CG) remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify a CG-associated transfer RNA-derived small RNA (tsRNA)-3012b pathway linking these processes. tsRNA-3012b was increased in clinical CG tissues, and angiogenin depletion reduced its abundance in CG-derived epithelial models. tsRNA-3012b promoted proliferation, increased NADPH availability, and shifted glutathione redox balance toward a more reduced state. Mechanistically, tsRNA-3012b interacted with insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA-binding protein 3 (IGF2BP3) and attenuated its association with an N7-methylguanosine (m7G)-associated region of branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase kinase (BCKDK) mRNA, thereby stabilizing BCKDK transcripts. Increased BCKDK promoted nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide kinase (NADK) phosphorylation at Ser103 and expanded the NADP(H) pool. Genetic disruption of BCKDK or NADK attenuated the associated NADP(H), roGFP2-Orp1, and proliferative phenotypes, and wild-type NADK restored these effects more effectively than NADK-S103A. During model induction, intravesical inhibition of tsRNA-3012b was associated with less CG-like epithelial remodeling, lower BCKDK abundance and NADK Ser/Thr phosphorylation, and a higher bladder-tissue NADP+/NADPH ratio. In CG-derived epithelial cells, tsRNA-3012b links NADK-dependent NADP(H) metabolism to proliferation.

title: Modeling the Codebase of Life.
abstract: Advances in computer hardware and simulation methodologies have transformed the study of biomolecular systems. Early descriptions of nucleic acids relied on simple polymer physics models that captured only large-scale behavior. Today, highly sophisticated atomistic and coarse-grained simulations enable detailed investigations of DNA, RNA, and their assemblies, revealing their structure, dynamics, mechanics, and interactions in biologically relevant environments across multiple spatial and temporal scales. Here, we review computational studies of nucleic acid systems, from early theoretical models to modern all-atom and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations. We highlight major methodological advances, review their applications to specific biomolecular systems, and discuss current challenges and future directions for computer simulations of nucleic acid systems.

title: Photothermal programming of CRISPR-Cas12a enables NIR-II imaging-guided LRRC15 editing for cancer and arthritis therapy.
abstract: Overexpression of leucine-rich repeat-containing protein 15 (LRRC15) is closely linked to cancer progression and rheumatoid arthritis (RA), making it a promising therapeutic target. Conventional single-target approaches suffer from limited efficacy and off-target effects. Here, we develop a dual-targeting nanoplatform based on Ag2S@ZIF-8 nanoparticles (NPs) and modified with hyaluronic acid (HA) for imaging-guided photothermal-gene editing synergistic therapy against LRRC15-related diseases. The resulting Ag2S-crRNA/Cas12a@ZIF-8@HA (ACZH) NPs deliver CRISPR RNA (crRNA) for sequence-specific LRRC15 recognition, together with HSP70 promoter-driven Cas12a plasmids. Ag2S NPs enable real-time NIR-II fluorescence imaging and generate localized hyperthermia (>42°C) that activates the HSP70 promoter to induce Cas12a expression and subsequent LRRC15 editing. In breast and lung cancer xenograft models, ACZH NPs achieve tumor inhibition rates of 81.37% and 82.5%, respectively; in an RA model, they reduce joint inflammation, prevent cartilage erosion, and promote bone repair. These findings offer a safe and effective strategy for LRRC15-related diseases.

title: Porcine Ear Necrosis Syndrome Temporally Associated with Mycotoxin Contamination of Corn in a Commercial Farrow-to-Finish Pig Farm.
abstract: Porcine Ear Necrosis Syndrome (PENS) is a multifactorial condition of increasing prevalence in intensive pig production systems worldwide. Mycotoxin contamination of feed has been proposed as one of several possible predisposing factors, through dermonecrotic and immunosuppressive mechanisms. This report describes the occurrence of PENS in weaned piglets at a commercial farrow-to-finish pig farm in central Greece, temporally associated with mycotoxin contamination of two successive corn batches. Screening of feed raw materials with quantitative lateral-flow immunoassays on 5 November 2025 detected T-2/HT-2 toxins at 333.8 ppb and fumonisins B1 + B2 at 2861 ppb in corn; analysis of a replacement corn batch on 12 January 2026 detected T-2/HT-2 at >600 ppb and deoxynivalenol (DON) at 623 ppb. Only the T-2/HT-2 concentrations exceeded the EU indicative level for unprocessed maize (200 ppb; approximately 1.7-fold and >3-fold, respectively), whereas fumonisin and DON concentrations were below the corresponding EU guidance values for maize. Complete feed was not analysed; based on 55.8% corn inclusion, the estimated dietary T-2/HT-2 concentrations were approximately 186 ppb and >335 ppb, but the actual dietary exposure of the piglets is unknown. In serological and molecular testing of 33 animals (individual sera by ELISA; nine pooled samples by PCR), no antibodies to or RNA of porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) and no Aujeszky's disease virus gE antibodies (one doubtful result) were detected; given the small number of animals sampled per production category, these results do not demonstrate freedom from either infection. Porcine circovirus type 2 (PCV2) DNA was detected by droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) in pooled sera from gilts before mating (1.23 × 104 copies/mL), piglets at 6 weeks (1.57 × 103 copies/mL) and finishers at 20 weeks (3.12 × 105 copies/mL), consistent with PCV2 field circulation despite piglet vaccination of unmonitored coverage. Affected cohorts additionally displayed increased aggression, cannibalism, and reciprocal ear biting, and necropsy of severely affected piglets revealed pulmonary oedema, gastric ulceration, and interstitial nephritis with cystitis; these lesions are non-specific and not characteristic of mycotoxicosis. These observations are consistent with mycotoxin exposure (particularly to T-2/HT-2), concurrent PCV2 circulation and ear biting being possible, potentially interacting contributing factors, whose relative contributions could not be determined. However, the single-farm design, the involvement of two different corn batches and the simultaneous implementation of several interventions do not allow a causal relationship or a primary causal agent to be established. Corn replacement, mycotoxin binder supplementation, dietary tryptophan (500 ppm) and vitamin E (150 ppm) supplementation, and optimisation of PCV2 vaccination coverage were implemented concurrently; thereafter, fewer new cases were observed on clinical follow-up, an outcome that is reported descriptively and cannot be attributed to any single measure.

title: An Optimized Convolutional Neural Network Framework for Cancer Classification Using RNA-Seq Transformation.
abstract: Inspired by the hierarchical, receptive-field-based processing of biological vision and by synaptic pruning in the developing brain, this work proposes a bio-inspired optimized convolutional neural network framework for multi-class cancer classification from RNA-Seq gene expression data. Although current deep learning models achieve strong predictive performance, existing approaches typically rely either on large pre-trained networks that cannot be deployed on resource-constrained devices or on image representations that normalize gene expression values to the 8-bit range (0-255), discarding the original biological dynamic range. A variance-driven feature selection step reduces 20,531 gene profiles to 16,384 high-information features, which are then reshaped into 128 × 128 images while preserving the original log2-normalized expression range (approximately 0-20.78) without rescaling to that 8-bit range. The network architecture is derived from a parametric mathematical model that enables analytical control over parameter count and FLOPs, resulting in a compact network with only 0.16 million parameters, a model size of 1.29 MB, and 0.0372 GFLOPs. On the TCGA PANCAN dataset (five cancer classes), the proposed baseline achieves 99.38% accuracy, matching or exceeding twelve state-of-the-art pre-trained architectures. For real-world deployment, the network was further optimized through two pathways: (A) direct TensorFlow Lite quantization in FP32, FP16, and INT8, and (B) structured channel pruning, analogous to synaptic pruning, followed by TFLite conversion. All variants retained the baseline 99.38% accuracy, with the Pruned TFLite FP16 variant reducing computational cost by 23.4% to 0.0285 GFLOPs, model size by 80.6%, and latency by 75.4%, while achieving the highest throughput of 1256 images/s at only 0.25 MB.

title: DNA methylation-dependent CDX1 enrichment at PVT1 exon 9 associated promoter drives overexpression of PVT1 exon 9 in aggressive prostate cancer.
abstract: Plasmacytoma variant translocation 1 (PVT1), a non-protein coding gene, is overexpressed in aggressive prostate cancer (PCa). Overexpression of PVT1 exon 9 has been demonstrated to induce malignant transformation of prostate epithelial cells and the development of aggressive PCa in vivo. However, the factors regulating overexpression and consequent oncogenicity of PVT1 exon 9 remain unclear. Here, we report the identification and functional characterization of a previously unrecognized internal regulatory element, the PVT1 exon 9 associated promoter (PEAP). We also demonstrate that its activity is governed by the caudal homeobox transcription factor CDX1 and local DNA methylation dynamics. While enzymatic methyl-sequence (EM-seq) profiling of PCa tissues and matched adjacent normal tissues revealed hypomethylation at PEAP in tumors, TFBind-based transcription factor motif prediction analysis revealed a discrete high-affinity CDX1 binding motif within PEAP. Using luciferase reporter assays, siRNA knockdown, CUT&RUN, CRISPR-based perturbation, isoform-specific droplet digital and quantitative PCR, we validated that the CDX1 motif within PEAP is functionally required for PEAP-driven induction of the oncogenic PVT1 exon 9 transcript. Moreover, CDX1 expression was significantly higher in aggressive PCa tissues compared to matched adjacent normal tissues in correlation with increased CDX1 occupancy at PEAP. Also, we uncovered enrichment of CDX1 at PEAP in PVT1 exon 9 overexpressing PCa cell lines, and increased CDX1 expression across PCa models overexpressing PVT1 exon 9. Targeting the predicted CDX1 binding motif within PEAP with a custom-designed antisense oligonucleotide disrupted CDX1 occupancy at PEAP, significantly inhibited expression of PVT1 exon 9, PCa cell proliferation and migration. Together, these results define a novel CDX1-PEAP signaling axis in which promoter methylation modulates CDX1 access to an internal regulatory element at PVT1, driving oncogenic PVT1 exon 9 overexpression. This work uncovers a novel regulatory mechanism in aggressive PCa and highlights the CDX1-PEAP axis as a potentially targetable node for therapeutic intervention in PVT1 exon 9 overexpressing aggressive PCa.

title: Silybin alleviates intestinal oxidative injury by orchestrating mitochondrial homeostasis and Nrf2 cytoprotection.
abstract: Oxidative stress is a key driver of intestinal disorders such as inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer. Silybin, a prominent flavonolignan derived from milk thistle, is known for its potent antioxidant properties, but exactly how it acts in the gut has remained unclear. This study aimed to investigate the protective effect of silybin against intestinal oxidative injury and to elucidate its underlying molecular mechanisms. We integrated RNA sequencing, biophysical binding analysis, and loss-of-function perturbations using paraquat (PQ)-induced intestinal oxidative injury model in piglets, nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2)-knockout mice, and intestinal epithelial (IPEC-J2) cells. Silybin effectively alleviated PQ-induced intestinal oxidative stress and barrier dysfunction by improving mitochondrial function and maintaining redox homeostasis. Mechanistic studies pointed to a restoration of oxidative phosphorylation and antioxidant gene networks upon silybin treatment. Specifically, silybin upregulated mitofusin 2 (MFN2) protein expression to promote mitochondrial fusion. The direct physical engagement between silybin and MFN2 was validated by molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and cellular thermal shift assay. Concurrently, silybin activated the Nrf2 pathway, increasing p-Nrf2 and HO-1 expression. Reciprocal perturbation experiments demonstrated that MFN2 knockdown reduced Nrf2 activity, while Nrf2 inhibition downregulated MFN2 protein, indicating a functional interdependence. Furthermore, genetic or pharmacological disruption of either MFN2 or Nrf2 completely abolished silybin's protective effects. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that silybin protects against intestinal oxidative injury by coordinating MFN2-mediated mitochondrial fusion and Nrf2-driven antioxidant defense. This dual-modulatory mechanism highlights silybin as a promising candidate for mitigating oxidative stress-associated intestinal conditions.

title: From mRNA Vaccines to In Vivo CAR-T Therapy: RNA-LNP Design and the Pharmacology of CAR-Positive Cells.
abstract: mRNA vaccines established scalable manufacturing and lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery for sequence-defined, non-integrating RNA medicines. In vivo CAR-T therapy repurposes this platform to generate CAR-positive lymphocytes after intravenous dosing, but its active product is a time-varying cell population rather than the injected RNA mass. This review critically examines the pharmacological sequence from biodistribution and cell-specific uptake to cytosolic RNA release, surface CAR expression, effector function, and disease response. The evidence comprises primary human T cells, mice, humanized mice, non-human primates, and 11 patients described in one correspondence and two meeting abstracts (as of July 2026). Matched studies show that receptor internalization can outweigh surface abundance, ligand density follows a non-monotonic relationship with delivery, and lipid chemistry and ligand presentation independently alter productive T-cell transfection. Preclinical models demonstrate transient CAR expression and target-cell depletion, whereas current human reports establish feasibility but not durable efficacy, a dose-response relationship, or the incidence of uncommon toxicities. We therefore distinguish administered dose, cell-resolved CAR-positive-cell exposure, and pharmacodynamic response, and propose their joint measurement as the basis for comparing platforms and selecting repeat-dose regimens.

title: HEPLISAV-B Breaks Immune Tolerance and Induces HBV Control via CD4 T Cell-Dependent Mechanism in Chronic HBV Mouse Model.
abstract: Background: Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection (CHB) affects nearly 300 million individuals globally and remains incurable with current antiviral therapies, which suppress viral replication but rarely achieve a functional cure, defined by sustained loss of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg). CHB is characterized by profound virus-induced immune tolerance that limits the efficacy of conventional therapeutic vaccination strategies. Objective: To evaluate the therapeutic efficacy and immunological mechanisms of HEPLISAV-B, a CpG-1018 adjuvanted HBsAg vaccine, in breaking immune tolerance and inducing functional cure-like responses in a murine model of CHB. Design: Using the adeno-associated virus-HBV (AAV-HBV) mouse model, mice with high levels of persistent HBV viremia were vaccinated with two doses of HEPLISAV-B. Virological outcomes in the blood and liver, immune responses and mechanisms were assessed. Results: HEPLISAV-B induced rapid and durable HBsAg clearance, markedly reduced circulating and intrahepatic HBV DNA and RNA, and suppressed viral replication without hepatocellular injury. Vaccination elicited robust, sustained anti-HBs IgG1 and IgA responses, enhanced HBsAg-specific T- and B-cell immunity, reduced CD4 regulatory T cells, and decreased PD-1 expression on CD4 T cells. Therapeutic efficacy was strictly dependent on CD4 T cells and the CD40/CD40L signaling pathway, but independent of CD8 T cells, indicating a CD4-driven, non-cytolytic antiviral mechanism critical for HEPLISAV-B-induced HBV control. Conclusions: HEPLISAV-B effectively breaks HBV-induced immune tolerance and restores coordinated antiviral immunity through a CD4 T cell/CD40L-dependent pathway. The findings support its potential as a therapeutic vaccine in CHB patients.

title: Sequential Disease-Modifying Therapy and Early Experience with Eplontersen in Hereditary Transthyretin Amyloidosis (p.Thr80Ala) with a Mixed Phenotype: A Case Report.
abstract: Background: Hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTRv) is a progressive multisystem disease, and some patients continue to deteriorate despite disease-modifying therapy. Real-world data on sequential treatment and on eplontersen after prior gene-silencing therapy are scarce. Case Presentation: A 60-year-old man with a family history suggestive of amyloidosis presented in early 2017 with heart failure (NYHA class II-III), chronic diarrhoea and carpal tunnel syndrome. Multimodality imaging, grade 3 bone scintigraphy, exclusion of a monoclonal protein (negative immunofixation and a normal serum free light chain ratio) and genetic testing established ATTRv amyloidosis due to the p.Thr80Ala variant, and colonic and duodenal biopsies showed gastrointestinal amyloid deposits. Between 2017 and 2025 he was treated sequentially with tafamidis, patisiran and vutrisiran. Over this period the disease progressed clinically, with weight loss, worsening axonal polyneuropathy on nerve conduction studies, rising NT-proBNP (up to 3808 pg/mL) and a decline in six-minute walk distance. In July 2025, vutrisiran was replaced by eplontersen. During 15 months of follow-up, eplontersen was well tolerated and body weight increased from 54 to 57 kg. NT-proBNP fluctuated without a sustained further rise (3093 pg/mL at the switch and 3141 pg/mL at 15 months), and troponin T and renal function were unchanged, whereas diarrhoea persisted and the six-minute walk distance was 360 m. Conclusions: This case shows clinical progression of p.Thr80Ala ATTRv amyloidosis despite sequential stabiliser and small interfering RNA therapy, followed by clinical stabilisation after a switch to eplontersen. Without serum TTR measurements and in a single patient, these observations do not allow conclusions about treatment efficacy.

title: Recent Advances in Duplex-Specific Nuclease-Assisted Biosensors: Mechanisms, Signal Strategies, and Biomedical Applications.
abstract: Duplex-specific nuclease (DSN) has emerged as a versatile enzymatic tool for highly sensitive nucleic-acid biosensing because it preferentially cleaves DNA in DNA/DNA and DNA/RNA duplexes while preserving RNA targets for repeated recycling. This review summarizes the catalytic characteristics and target-recycling mechanism of DSN and discusses the classical design principles that govern probe architecture, reaction conditions, and sensing interfaces. Major signal-transduction strategies, including fluorescence, electrochemical, colorimetric, electrochemiluminescence, surface-enhanced Raman scattering, and photoelectrochemical approaches, are considered with emphasis on their fundamental advantages and limitations. Particular attention is given to microRNA detection, single-nucleotide discrimination, cancer biomarkers, liquid biopsy, infectious-disease testing, and point-of-care applications. Analytical performance is discussed in the context of sensitivity, selectivity, reproducibility, matrix effects, and comparison with established amplification methods. Finally, the principal barriers to translation-including nonspecific adsorption, limited compatibility with untreated clinical samples, insufficient standardization, and incomplete clinical validation-are summarized. Future progress will depend on simplified probe architectures, robust antifouling interfaces, integrated sample processing, multiplexed readout, and standardized validation rather than amplification complexity alone.

title: Fis family members synergistically control the virulence of Legionella pneumophila.
abstract: Legionella pneumophila virulence is controlled in a growth phase-dependent manner by a complex regulatory network involving several two-component systems, small regulatory RNAs, and the translational CsrA regulator. Here, we address the additional role of nucleoid-associated protein (NAP) regulators in this network by investigating the regulatory functions of the three Fis proteins (Fis1, Fis2, and Fis3), a unique feature among bacteria, in the infection cycle of L. pneumophila. Specifically, we show that deletion of fis1 has a major impact on L. pneumophila virulence and that deletion of fis2 enhances the intensity of this phenotype. Consistently, RNA-seq analysis and reporter gene fusions demonstrate the predominant role of Fis1 in the regulation of many virulence-related genes, including those involved in the flagellum, pilus biosynthesis, and Dot/Icm type 4 secretion machinery, as well as many genes encoding Dot/Icm effectors. Both Fis1 and Fis2 bind to AT-rich motifs upstream of their target genes, but Fis1 has higher affinity than Fis2. Importantly, Fis1 and Fis2 would be capable of forming heterodimers that could bind with variable affinity to this AT-rich motif. It is also important to note that the three Fis proteins are not produced at the same time and in the same amounts. We therefore hypothesize that the duplication of fis genes in L. pneumophila is not simply a backup system to compensate for potentially deleterious mutations in a fis gene but rather is a means to fine-tune the expression of targeted genes, particularly virulence genes. Appropriate control of virulence gene expression is crucial to the success of bacterial infection. Nucleoid-associated protein regulators, including Fis proteins, have been shown to participate in the virulence of several human pathogens. The importance of our discovery lies in the fact that Legionella pneumophila possesses three non-homologous Fis proteins instead of just one. We demonstrate that Fis1 and Fis2 are not functional duplicates of each other. On the contrary, Fis1 and Fis2 are synthesized neither simultaneously nor in equal amounts during the bacterial growth phase, and they cooperate to regulate virulence gene expression by targeting similar AT-rich motifs, albeit with distinct affinity, and by being capable of forming heterodimers.
